If it’s bothering you, pulling your attention, or creating pressure, it earns a row.  How to write the problem (this is key)  Write it as a clear, factual sentence—not a feeling, not a rant.  Bad:  “Everything is a mess”  “I’m overwhelmed”  “This situation is impossible”  Good:  “Property tax issue on [address] not resolved”  “Avoiding follow-up call with lender”  “Admin backlog from last two weeks”  “Sleep inconsistency affecting training”  If you can’t write it cleanly in one sentence, the problem is still fog. This step is about externalizing, not fixing.  Think of each row as saying to your brain:  “I see you. You’re captured. You don’t need to shout anymore.”  That’s why anxiety drops when you do this.  What happens next (so you don’t hesitate)  After you list the problems:  Move to the numbers (Impact, Urgency, Leverage, Emotional Weight)  Let the sheet calculate priority  Sort by priority  Pick one for today’s 20-minute siege  But none of that happens until the problem is listed.  The rule to remember  If a problem is:  in your head → it owns you  on the sheet → you own it  So open the backlog now and start filling Column A. No ranking. No fixing. Just capture.  Once the list is out of your head and on paper, the pressure changes shape—and that’s when control comes back.
